issues.legal_issue: A grant authorizing a municipality to sell government land does not, without more, transfer ownership of that land to the municipality.
material_facts: The lands had been used or occupied by the former state's forces and were treated as government property when the former state was integrated into the Indian Union.
The resolutions gave municipalities the right to sell government land within municipal limits and to collect specified income from it.

Later government directions retained conditions on the municipality's exercise of that right, and the government cancelled the authorization before subsequently reconsidering it subject to conditions.
The municipality did not take possession of the disputed land.
issues.conclusion: The resolutions authorized the municipality to execute sales of government land on the government's behalf; they did not vest title to the disputed land in the municipality.
issues.legal_principle: Following accession and territorial and financial integration, land and buildings used or occupied by former Indian State Governments, as distinct from rulers' private property, vested in the Government of India. The resolutions must be understood in that context: they transferred authority to sell government land, not ownership. The Court relied on the integration history and the text and subsequent treatment of the resolutions; it cited no earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The claimant brings a suit for possession on the basis of an asserted title.
predicates.former_state_government_land: The disputed land belonged to a former state government rather than being the ruler's private property.
predicates.land_used_or_occupied_by_former_state_fo: The former state's forces used or occupied the disputed land.
predicates.municipal_authorization_to_sell_governme: The municipality received authority to sell government land, rather than an express transfer of ownership.

issues.definition: When a title-based possession suit concerns former state government land used or occupied by its forces and the municipality received authority to sell that land, the authorization does not itself transfer title to the municipality.

issues.legal_issue: In a suit for possession based on title governed by the applicable title-based limitation rule, the court must determine the claimant's title even if the defendant has not pleaded adverse possession.
material_facts: The municipality filed its possession suit after the Limitation Act, 1963 had come into force.
The suit sought possession on the basis of the municipality's asserted title, which the defendants denied.
The defendants had not pleaded adverse possession.
issues.conclusion: Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applied, and the court had to decide whether the municipality had title even though the defendants had not pleaded adverse possession.
issues.legal_principle: Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applied to the suit for possession based on title. Because the defendants denied the claimant's title, the court had to determine title notwithstanding the absence of a plea of adverse possession. The Court cited no earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The claimant brings a suit for possession on the basis of an asserted title.
predicates.suit_filed_after_limitation_law_commence: The suit was filed after the applicable limitation law came into force.
predicates.defendant_denied_claimant_title: The defendant denied that the claimant held title to the disputed property.

issues.definition: If a claimant brings a title-based possession suit after the applicable limitation law has commenced and the defendant denies the claimant's title, the court must determine whether the claimant has title.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who has not proved title cannot rely on the principle that possession follows title when the defendant is in physical possession, and the defendant need not plead or prove adverse possession.
material_facts: The municipality did not prove title to the disputed land.
Evidence showed that the defendants had physical possession of the land.
The municipality relied on the principle that possession follows title.
issues.conclusion: The municipality could not rely on possession following title, and because it had not proved title in its possession suit, the defendants did not need to plead or prove adverse possession.
issues.legal_principle: The principle that possession follows title could not assist a claimant that had not established title where evidence showed physical possession by the defendant. In a suit for possession based on title, failure to prove the claimant's title made it unnecessary for the defendant to plead or prove adverse possession. The Court cited no earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The claimant brings a suit for possession on the basis of an asserted title.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_title: The claimant did not establish title to the disputed property.
predicates.defendant_in_physical_possession: The defendant was in physical possession of the disputed property.

issues.definition: In a title-based possession suit, when the claimant fails to establish title and the defendant is in physical possession, the defendant need not plead or prove adverse possession.
